value: feeling safe, from the patient's perspective, in a perioperative context
what feeling safe means for patients in a perioperative setting
a definition of feeling safe with three attributes, two antecedents and two consequences

quote: The eight-step concept analysis approach proposed by Walker and Avant was utilized to examine the attributes of feeling safe
In this study, the attributes of feeling safe are established as Participation, Control, and Presence

value: patients' perceived feeling of safety around surgery
quote: For patients, the perceived feeling of safety may be just as important as the fact of actually being safe throughout a procedure
None
For the purpose of this paper, “feeling safe” is defined in accordance with the definition of the Swedish word trygghet : a person that does not feel worried or threatened

Participation and inclusion in care and decision-making (Aasa et al., 2013 ; Cudré et al., 2015 ; Gustafsson et al., 2010 ; Haapala et al., 2013 ) was the most frequently used characteristic when describing feeling safe in a perioperative context

The second attribute of feeling safe is Control, which includes ability to trust the staff, their abilities, and competence, as well as to feel like that the staff are in control and supportive and that they are looking after the patient
The last attribute of feeling safe in a perioperative setting is Presence, and it can mean both presence of family and presence of staff

The internal dimension is linked to early childhood experiences and continues to grow throughout one’s life; it is described as a feeling of warmth, harmony, calm, and trust, and it includes the ability to believe in oneself and confess one’s flaws
The external dimension of feeling safe is comprised of knowledge, control, and trustworthy individuals, and it is influenced by the person’s surroundings
Patient safety can be defined as the absence of unintentional injury
Psychological safety is a related concept that has been described in different areas
Feeling acknowledged involves patients’ desire to be seen as a person, not just a patient
The primary antecedents that need to be fulfilled before patients feel safe in a perioperative context are Knowledge and Relationship
Thus, person-centred care could make patients feel a greater sense of participation, control and presence, that is, feeling safe in a perioperative context
According to Walker and Avant ( 2011 ), antecedents are the events or incidents that need to take place before the concept occurs

Consequences are the outcomes of the concept (Walker & Avant, 2011 ). The literature establishes the consequences of the concept of feeling safe in a perioperative context as Feeling Acknowledged and Trust
Empirical referents are a way of recognizing or measuring the defining attributes of a concept, thereby determining its existence
A relationship with the staff promotes patients’ feelings of safety and helps them realize that they do not need to be in complete control of the situation and that they are not alone
During surgery, when patients cede control of their body to the staff, there is a risk that the patient feels insecure and has a fear of being abandoned
